whyItMatters: A UI can show text as it is generated, and the SDKs require streaming for large `max_tokens` values to avoid HTTP timeouts.
example: Events: `message_start`, `content_block_delta`s, `message_delta`, `message_stop`. Show each `text_delta` as it arrives.

definition: Setting `strict: true` on a tool definition constrains sampling so Claude's tool inputs strictly follow the tool's `input_schema`.
whyItMatters: Without it, Claude might send `"2"` instead of `2` or omit required fields. With it, there's no need to validate and retry tool calls.
example: Add `"strict": true` at the top level of the tool, alongside `name`, `description` and `input_schema`.

definition: The agent regularly writes notes to memory outside its context window; the notes are pulled back into context at later times.
whyItMatters: It gives persistent memory with minimal overhead, and Anthropic says it excels for iterative development with clear milestones.
example: A custom agent maintaining a `NOTES.md` file to track progress across a complex task.

source.title: Effective context engineering for AI agents

definition: Constrains Claude's responses to a schema so output is valid and parseable. Two features: **JSON outputs** (`output_config.format`) for the response, and **strict tool use** (`strict: true`) for tool inputs.
whyItMatters: It removes JSON parse errors, missing fields and retries for schema violations. Still check `stop_reason`: a `refusal` or `max_tokens` stop can return output that doesn't match the schema.
example: `output_config: {format: {type: "json_schema", schema: {...}}}` to extract name, email and plan interest from a sales email.

definition: A specialized assistant that handles one kind of task in its own context window, with a custom system prompt, specific tool access and independent permissions, and returns only a summary.
whyItMatters: Use one when a side task would flood your context with logs or search results, or to restrict tools. Stay in the main conversation for iterative back-and-forth or when latency matters.
example: Use a subagent to run the test suite and report only the failing tests with their error messages.

definition: A non-fork subagent starts fresh: its own system prompt plus the Agent tool's prompt, without the parent's history. Only its final message returns.
whyItMatters: The Agent tool's prompt string is the only content passed from parent to subagent, so include file paths, errors and decisions in it.
example: A doc-reviewer subagent limited to Read and Grep can analyze files but never modify them.

definition: What a lead agent gives each subagent: an objective, an output format, guidance on the tools and sources to use, and clear task boundaries.
whyItMatters: Without detailed task descriptions, subagents duplicate work, leave gaps or fail to find necessary information.
example: Not just "research the semiconductor shortage", but a scoped objective, sources and output format.

source.title: How we built our multi-agent research system

definition: The measurable targets an LLM app must meet. Good criteria are **specific**, **measurable**, **achievable** and **relevant** to the app's purpose and users.
whyItMatters: An LLM app starts with clear criteria, then evals that measure them. Instead of "good performance", specify e.g. an F1 of at least 0.85 on a held-out test set.
example: Bad: "Safe outputs". Good: < 0.1% of 10,000 trials flagged for toxicity by the content filter.

source.title: Define success criteria and build evaluations

definition: The top-level Messages API field for instructions that apply from the start of a conversation, such as a goal or role.
whyItMatters: Put standing instructions in the top-level `system` field: a `system` message can't be the first entry in `messages`.
example: Some newer models (e.g. Claude Opus 5.5) also accept `"role": "system"` messages after a user turn.

definition: A parameter that controls the randomness of a model's predictions during text generation.
whyItMatters: Lower values suit analytical tasks, higher ones creative tasks. Deprecated: models released after Claude Opus 4.6 accept only 1.0 and reject other values with a 400 error.
example: On an older model, use `temperature` near 0.0 for multiple choice and near 1.0 for brainstorming; on current models, leave it unset.

definition: The `display` field of the thinking config. `"summarized"` returns a summary of Claude's reasoning; `"omitted"` (the default on many models) returns thinking blocks with an empty `thinking` field. Billing is the same.
whyItMatters: Set `"omitted"` when your app doesn't show thinking: text starts streaming sooner. It lowers latency, not cost, since you're still charged for the full thinking tokens.
example: A chat UI that shows Claude's reasoning sends `thinking: {"type": "adaptive", "display": "summarized"}`; a backend job leaves it `"omitted"`.

definition: The time from sending the prompt until the model generates the first token of its response.
whyItMatters: Particularly relevant with streaming, when you want a responsive experience. Baseline latency instead covers processing the prompt and generating the response.
example: A chat app streams responses so users see output as soon as the first token arrives, rather than waiting for the complete reply.

definition: The smallest unit a language model works in: a word, subword, character or byte. The glossary puts a Claude token at approximately 3.5 English characters.
whyItMatters: Costs, limits and context use are counted in tokens, and the ratio to characters depends on the model and language. Use token counting with the model you plan to use instead of estimating.
example: Claude 4.7 and later models produce approximately 30 percent more tokens for the same text than earlier models, so recount before switching.

definition: The algorithm the API uses for rate limiting: capacity is continuously replenished up to your maximum, rather than reset at fixed intervals.
whyItMatters: Limits can apply over shorter intervals: 60 requests per minute might be enforced as 1 per second, so short bursts can trigger 429s.
example: Spread 60 requests across the minute instead of sending them all in the first second.

definition: `POST /v1/messages/count_tokens` returns an input-token estimate for Messages inputs, except most server tools, the MCP connector and URL or file sources.
whyItMatters: It is free, with its own RPM limits. Count under the model you'll use: Claude 4.7+ tokenizers yield about 30% more tokens than earlier models.
example: Before a migration, count one request under each model and compare the two `input_tokens` values.

definition: Optional MCP hints about tool behavior, e.g. `readOnlyHint` (doesn't modify its environment) or `destructiveHint`. Clients must treat them as untrusted unless the server is trusted.
whyItMatters: They're hints, not guarantees: never skip a confirmation just because an untrusted server marks a tool `readOnlyHint: true`.
example: `"annotations": {"readOnlyHint": false, "destructiveHint": false, "idempotentHint": true}` for a tool that only adds data and is safe to repeat.

definition: A request field that controls tool calling: **auto** (Claude decides), **any** (must use one of the tools), **tool** (must use the named tool) or **none**.
whyItMatters: `any` and `tool` fail on Claude Opus 5.5, Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1, and with manual extended thinking; use `auto`, with strict tool use for schema-valid inputs.
example: `{"type": "tool", "name": "get_weather"}` forces that tool where supported.

definition: A user-defined tool entry: a **name** matching `^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,128}$`, a detailed plaintext **description**, and an `input_schema` (a JSON Schema object).
whyItMatters: The API builds a special system prompt from your tool definitions. Each optional `input_examples` entry must match `input_schema`, or you get a 400.
example: `get_weather` with a required `location` string and an optional `unit` of "celsius" or "fahrenheit".

definition: The content block your app sends on the next request with a tool's output, answering a `tool_use` block. Claude never sees your implementation, only the schema and the result.
whyItMatters: Every client tool call is a round trip: the loop only continues once you send the result back. Server tools such as `web_search` never need one, because Anthropic runs them.
example: Claude's `tool_use` asks for a database query; your app runs it and sends the rows back as a `tool_result` block in a user message on the next request.

definition: A context editing strategy, `clear_tool_uses_20250919`, that clears the oldest tool results once context passes a threshold, leaving placeholder text.
whyItMatters: Fits agents with heavy tool use whose old results are no longer needed. Defaults: trigger at **100,000** input tokens, keep the **3** most recent tool uses.
example: List a tool in `exclude_tools` if its uses and results must never be cleared.

definition: A beta SDK helper that runs your tools when Claude calls them, sends results back and manages conversation state until Claude stops calling tools.
whyItMatters: For human-in-the-loop approval, custom logging or conditional execution, use the manual loop instead.
example: Python: tools use `@beta_tool`; `runner.until_done()` gets the final message.

definition: Lets Claude work with hundreds or thousands of tools: tools marked `defer_loading: true` stay out of context until Claude searches the catalog and loads only the ones it needs.
whyItMatters: Loading every definition up front bloats context, and Claude's tool selection degrades as the tool count grows. At least one tool, normally the tool search tool itself, must stay non-deferred.
example: Add `{"type": "tool_search_tool_regex_20251119", "name": "tool_search_tool_regex"}` and set `defer_loading: true` on the rest.

definition: Lets Claude call functions you define or Anthropic provides. Claude decides when to call a tool from the request and the tool description, then returns a structured call that your app (client tools) or Anthropic (server tools) runs.
whyItMatters: With the default `tool_choice` of `{"type": "auto"}`, Claude decides each turn whether to call a tool. To require a call rather than rely on prompting, set `tool_choice`.
example: `tools: [{"type": "web_search_20260209", "name": "web_search"}]`: Anthropic runs the search and returns cited results in the same response.

definition: The response content block Claude emits to call a tool: the tool name plus a JSON object of arguments. Your app runs the operation and sends the output back in a `tool_result` block.
whyItMatters: A response with `stop_reason: "tool_use"` means your app must run the call and reply. If you're writing a regex to extract a decision from prose, it should have been a tool call.
example: Loop while `stop_reason == "tool_use"`: execute each `tool_use` block, send back `tool_result` blocks, and repeat until another stop reason.

definition: A hook output field: in a `PreToolUse` hook it replaces the tool's arguments before the tool runs.
whyItMatters: It replaces the entire input object, so include unchanged fields alongside modified ones. Permission rules are evaluated against the input your hook returns, not the one Claude sent.
example: A `PreToolUse` hook returns `permissionDecision: "allow"` with `updatedInput` holding the answer, so `AskUserQuestion` runs without prompting.

definition: The Claude Code hook event that fires when a prompt is submitted, before Claude processes it.
whyItMatters: Use it to validate or block prompts, or add context, before Claude sees them. It runs before every prompt and blocks processing until done, so a stuck hook stalls the session.
example: Return `{"decision": "block", "reason": "..."}` to stop a prompt; the reason is shown to the user and isn't added to Claude's context.

definition: A server tool that lets Claude retrieve the full content of specified web pages and PDF documents. You pay only standard token costs for the fetched content.
whyItMatters: With untrusted input alongside sensitive data it's an exfiltration risk. Claude can only fetch URLs already in the conversation; `allowed_domains` and `max_uses` narrow it further.
example: `tools=[{"type": "web_fetch_20250910", "name": "web_fetch", "max_uses": 5}]`, then "Summarize this article: <url>".

definition: A server tool giving Claude real-time web content, so it can answer with up-to-date information beyond its knowledge cutoff. Responses include citations for the sources used.
whyItMatters: Cap searches per request with `max_uses`, and scope sources with `allowed_domains` or `blocked_domains`, not both (a 400 error). When showing output to end users, include the citations.
example: `tools=[{"type": "web_search_20250305", "name": "web_search", "max_uses": 5, "allowed_domains": ["example.com"]}]`

definition: An API for a two-way interactive session between browser and server: either side can send messages without the client polling for replies.
whyItMatters: The stable `WebSocket` interface has no backpressure: if messages arrive faster than you process them, the client can fill memory or max out CPU. `WebSocketStream` handles backpressure but is non-standard.
example: Close a page's WebSocket when the user is done with it: an open connection may stop the browser from adding the page to the bfcache.

definition: **Workflows** run LLMs and tools through predefined code paths. **Agents** let the LLM dynamically direct its own process and tool use.
whyItMatters: Workflows give predictability for well-defined tasks; agents give flexibility at the cost of latency and spend. Start with the simplest solution.
example: A fixed translate → check → format pipeline is a workflow; an assistant that decides which files to edit is an agent.

definition: A way to organize API usage within an organization, separating projects, environments or teams while keeping centralized billing and administration.
whyItMatters: Give each project or environment its own API keys, members, rate limits and spend limits. A key scoped to one workspace can only access resources in that workspace.
example: An admin creates a `Production` workspace via `client.organization.workspaces.create(name="Production")`, then caps its monthly spend under **Spend limits**.

definition: A request header carrying your API key from the Console. It is the legacy fallback for the `Authorization: Bearer` header, and is still supported.
whyItMatters: Raw HTTP calls need either it or `Authorization: Bearer`; the SDKs send the authentication header for you, so you set it by hand only outside an SDK.
example: A raw request sends `x-api-key: <your Console API key>` together with `anthropic-version: 2023-06-01`.

definition: Wrapping each type of prompt content in its own tag, such as `<instructions>` or `<context>`, so Claude can parse a complex prompt unambiguously.
whyItMatters: Reduces misinterpretation when instructions, context, examples and variable inputs share one prompt. Use consistent, descriptive tag names.
example: Nest for hierarchy: `<documents>` holds each `<document index="1">`, with its source and content in their own tags.

definition: **ZDR**: an arrangement under which Anthropic doesn't store prompts or responses at rest after the API response returns. Enabled per organization, for eligible features only.
whyItMatters: Check the feature eligibility table. Under ZDR, the API does **not** block features marked "No" (often stateful ones); using one steps outside your ZDR arrangement for that data.
example: A ZDR organization can't call the API from browser code via CORS, so its web app routes requests through a backend proxy server.

definition: How the model picks each next token from its options. `temperature` sets how much randomness is injected; `top_k` samples only from the top K options, and `top_p` (nucleus sampling) cuts options off at a cumulative probability.
whyItMatters: Sampling is why the same prompt can come back worded differently. Models released after Claude Opus 4.6 reject any `temperature` other than 1.0, any `top_p` below 0.99, and any `top_k`, with a 400 error.
example: On an older model, `"top_k": 5` samples each next token from only the 5 most likely options.

definition: Prompting with instructions only: the prompt contains no example of the task.
whyItMatters: It's the baseline the other modes add to. In one Anthropic study, a model that couldn't do a task zero-shot managed it once a single example was added (one-shot).
example: "Classify this ticket as billing, bug or other." with no sample tickets in the prompt.

definition: Prompting with a single example of the task added to the instructions.
whyItMatters: It sits between zero-shot (no example) and few-shot (several examples). In one Anthropic study, adding a single example let a model do a task it couldn't do zero-shot.
example: The ticket-classification instructions plus one `<example>` showing a ticket and its label.

definition: An eval in which a model grades another model's output, returning a specific result such as "correct"/"incorrect" or a 1–5 score.
whyItMatters: Fast, flexible and scalable for complex judgments; test its reliability before scaling. Give it a detailed rubric and thinking on, and generally use a different model from the one being graded.
example: Rubric in `<rubric>`, answer in `<answer>`, then "Output 'correct' or 'incorrect' in <result> tags."

source.title: Define success criteria and build evaluations

definition: The Claude API is a RESTful API at `https://api.anthropic.com`: you send JSON over HTTP to endpoints such as `POST /v1/messages`, with auth, `anthropic-version` and `content-type` headers.
whyItMatters: The client SDKs call this same API but send the headers and handle retries, errors, streaming and timeouts for you. Without an SDK, that's your code's job.
example: `POST https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages` with `x-api-key`, `anthropic-version: 2023-06-01` and `content-type: application/json`.

definition: The `signature` field on a thinking block: an opaque, encrypted copy of Claude's full reasoning. The API uses it to verify the block was generated by Claude when you pass it back.
whyItMatters: Pass it back exactly as received and never parse it. When streaming, it arrives as one `signature_delta` just before the block's `content_block_stop`, so a block saved earlier lacks it.
example: With `display: "omitted"` a thinking block has an empty `thinking` field but a long `signature`, which still carries the reasoning for the next turn.

definition: A block the API may return when part of Claude's reasoning is safety-redacted. It holds encrypted thinking in a `data` field and has no readable text.
whyItMatters: It falls under the carry-back rule like any thinking block: during tool use, send it back unchanged and in its original position. Dropping it because it looks empty breaks the rule.
example: Assistant content `[thinking, redacted_thinking, tool_use]` goes back exactly in that order, followed by your `tool_result`.

definition: Thinking between tool calls within one assistant turn, so Claude can reason about each tool result before deciding what to do next.
whyItMatters: With adaptive thinking it's automatic, with no beta header. On models using manual extended thinking, interleaving requires a beta header.
example: An agent calls `search`, thinks about the results, then calls `fetch_page` with a better-chosen URL.

definition: The delta type inside a `content_block_delta` event that carries the next fragment of a `text` block's text.
whyItMatters: Append each fragment to the block with the same `index`. The text is only complete after that block's `content_block_stop`.
example: `{"type": "content_block_delta", "index": 0, "delta": {"type": "text_delta", "text": "ello frien"}}`

definition: The delta type that streams the `thinking` field of a thinking block. A single `signature_delta` follows just before the block's `content_block_stop`.
whyItMatters: With `display: "omitted"` you get one `thinking_delta` with an empty string, so a live reasoning pane stays empty by design.
example: `{"type": "thinking_delta", "thinking": "1071 = 2 × 462 + 147"}` inside a `content_block_delta` event.

definition: How strict tool use (and structured outputs) works: the model's token sampling is constrained to outputs that are valid against your JSON Schema.
whyItMatters: It's why strict mode is a guarantee rather than a request: functions receive correctly-typed arguments every time, with no need to validate and retry tool calls.
example: With `"strict": true`, a `passengers` field typed as an integer always comes back as `2`, never `"two"`.

definition: An event of type `ping` that may appear any number of times in a streamed Messages response. It carries no content.
whyItMatters: A handler should accept pings anywhere in the stream and ignore them, not treat them as errors or as a sign that a block is ready.
example: `event: ping` / `data: {"type": "ping"}` arriving between `content_block_start` and the first `content_block_delta`.

definition: A content block of type `text` holding natural language. In tool use, Claude's response can include one before its `tool_use` block; in your reply, text goes after all `tool_result` blocks.
whyItMatters: Assistant messages hold Claude's `text` and `tool_use` blocks; user messages hold your `tool_result` blocks. In a user message with tool results, a text block placed before a `tool_result` causes a 400 error.
example: Claude: `{"type": "text", "text": "I'll check the weather."}` then a `tool_use` block. Your reply: the `tool_result`, then optionally a text block.

definition: The plaintext `description` in a tool definition: what the tool does, when to use it (and when not), what each parameter means, and its caveats.
whyItMatters: Anthropic calls detailed descriptions by far the most important factor in tool performance: the more context Claude has, the better it decides when and how to use a tool. Aim for at least 3–4 sentences.
example: Good: "Retrieves the current stock price for a given ticker symbol… It will not provide any other information about the stock or company." Poor: "Gets the stock price for a ticker."

definition: An optional tool-definition field: an array of example input objects showing Claude well-formed calls, such as when to include optional parameters and which formats to use.
whyItMatters: Use it for complex, nested or format-sensitive inputs, after writing a clear description. Each example must be valid against `input_schema`, or the request returns a 400; examples also add prompt tokens.
example: `get_weather` with `[{"location": "Tokyo, Japan", "unit": "celsius"}, {"location": "New York, NY"}]`: the second shows `unit` is optional.

definition: The MCP request a client sends to discover a server's tools. Each tool in the response has a `name`, a `title`, a `description` and an `inputSchema`.
whyItMatters: This is how an MCP server replaces hand-written schemas: the application combines the listed tools from every connected server into one registry the model can use.
example: A weather server's `tools/list` returns `weather_current` with a required `location` and an optional `units` that defaults to "metric".

definition: The MCP request a client sends to run a discovered tool, with the tool's exact `name` and `arguments` matching its `inputSchema`. The server returns a `content` array.
whyItMatters: When the model decides to call an MCP tool, the AI application routes the call to the right server with `tools/call` and returns the result to the model.
example: `{"method": "tools/call", "params": {"name": "weather_current", "arguments": {"location": "San Francisco", "units": "imperial"}}}`

definition: Grouping related tools under common prefixes, by service (`asana_search`, `jira_search`) or by resource (`asana_projects_search`), so each tool's boundary is clear.
whyItMatters: When tools overlap in function or have a vague purpose, agents get confused about which one to use. Prefixes help Claude pick the right tool as the tool set grows across many servers.
example: Rename two `search` tools from different MCP servers to `asana_search` and `jira_search`.

source.title: Writing effective tools for agents — with agents

definition: Keeping low-signal tokens out of context in the first place: tools return only what the agent needs, using pagination, range selection, filtering or truncation with sensible defaults.
whyItMatters: Tool responses can use up lots of context. Trimming them at the source leaves less to clear or summarize later.
example: Claude Code restricts tool responses to 25,000 tokens by default; a concise `response_format` used about a third of the tokens of a detailed one.

source.title: Writing effective tools for agents — with agents

definition: Splitting a knowledge base into smaller chunks of text before embedding and indexing them for retrieval.
whyItMatters: The choice of chunk size, chunk boundary and chunk overlap can affect retrieval performance, and a chunk cut from its document can lose the context that makes it findable.
example: "The company's revenue grew by 3% over the previous quarter." On its own, this chunk doesn't say which company or which period.

definition: Prepending a short, chunk-specific context (usually 50–100 tokens, written by Claude) to each chunk before embedding it and building the BM25 index.
whyItMatters: In Anthropic's tests it cut the top-20 retrieval failure rate by 35% (embeddings), 49% (plus BM25) and 67% (plus reranking).
example: "This chunk is from an SEC filing on ACME corp's performance in Q2 2023; the previous quarter's revenue was $314 million." is prepended to the chunk.

definition: **Best Matching 25**: a ranking function that uses lexical matching to find precise word or phrase matches.
whyItMatters: Semantic embeddings can find content about error codes in general yet miss the exact one; BM25 alongside embeddings catches exact identifiers.
example: A query for "Error code TS-999" needs the page that names TS-999, not just pages about error codes.

definition: A filtering step that scores retrieved chunks against the query so only the most relevant are passed to the model.
whyItMatters: It trades cost for quality: reranking more chunks performs better, reranking fewer keeps latency and cost lower.
example: Retrieve candidates with embeddings and BM25, rerank them, then pass the top 20 to Claude.

definition: A Voyage AI embedding parameter that marks text as a `query` or a `document`, so a retrieval-specific prompt is prepended before embedding.
whyItMatters: For RAG and other retrieval tasks, the Embeddings guide says not to omit it: it can create better vectors and better retrieval quality.
example: Index with `input_type="document"`; embed each user question with `input_type="query"`.

definition: A 28×28-pixel patch of an image. An image costs ⌈width / 28⌉ × ⌈height / 28⌉ visual tokens, after any downscaling to the model's limits.
whyItMatters: Estimate image cost before you build: tokens × input price × image count. High-resolution models can use up to roughly 3× more tokens per image.
example: A 1000×1000 image is 36 × 36 = 1,296 visual tokens; caps are 4,784 (Claude 4.7+) and 1,568 (standard tier).

definition: A point where an agent pauses for a person's input before going on. In the Agent SDK, `canUseTool` fires for tool calls that aren't auto-approved and pauses execution until your app returns allow or deny.
whyItMatters: Calls approved earlier, by an allow rule or a mode like `acceptEdits` or `bypassPermissions`, never reach the callback. For a check on every call, use a `PreToolUse` hook.
example: Every `Bash` command reaches `canUseTool`, which shows it in your UI; a denial's message tells Claude why, so it can adjust.

definition: An Agent SDK tool Claude calls to ask the user clarifying questions with multiple-choice options. It triggers your `canUseTool` callback, where you show the questions and return the answers.
whyItMatters: Claude writes the questions; you can't add your own to this flow. If you restrict `tools`, include `AskUserQuestion`, and note it isn't currently available in subagents spawned via the Agent tool.
example: In `plan` mode Claude asks "Which database should I use?" with 2–4 options; your UI returns the chosen label.

definition: How an agent is wired up: a raw Messages API loop you write yourself, the Claude Agent SDK running in a process you operate, or Claude Managed Agents, where Anthropic hosts the harness and runs the loop.
whyItMatters: The agent pattern stays the same; the path decides who runs the loop and what you build yourself, such as tool execution, sandboxing and hosting.
example: Writing your own tool loop: raw API. Claude Code's tools inside your service: Agent SDK. Anthropic-hosted harness and sandbox: Managed Agents.

definition: Memory held in the context window itself: the system prompt, conversation history and tool inputs and outputs. Within an Agent SDK session it doesn't reset between turns; everything accumulates.
whyItMatters: It ends with the conversation and grows every turn; large tool outputs can use thousands of tokens in one turn.
example: A support chat keeps the customer's order number in its history for the rest of that conversation, and loses it when a new one starts.

definition: Keeping a long session going by replacing older history with a summary, which the Agent SDK does automatically (compaction) when the context window approaches its limit.
whyItMatters: Specific instructions from early in the conversation may not survive the summary. Put standing rules in CLAUDE.md, which is re-injected on every request.
example: Add a CLAUDE.md section telling the compactor to preserve the task objective and the file paths read or modified.

definition: Skills listed in a subagent's `skills` field. The full content of each is injected into the subagent's context at startup, not just the description.
whyItMatters: A subagent doesn't see skills invoked in the main session. The field controls preloading, not access: unlisted skills stay invocable via the Skill tool unless you remove that tool.
example: `skills: [api-conventions]` in `.claude/agents/api-developer.md` gives that subagent the conventions from its first turn.
